content: The document titled Standards for Prosthetics and Orthotics outlines a comprehensive framework for the development and implementation of high-quality, affordable prosthetics and orthotics services globally. It is divided into two parts: the standards themselves and an implementation manual. These standards aim to ensure that prosthetics and orthotics services are accessible, people-centered, and responsive to the unique needs of individuals and their environments. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that prosthetics (artificial limbs) and orthotics (braces and splints) are essential for enabling individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations to lead healthy, independent, and dignified lives. These devices allow individuals to participate in education, employment, and social activities, while also reducing the need for long-term healthcare and caregiver support. However, access to these devices remains limited, with only 1 in 10 people in need currently able to obtain them due to high costs, lack of awareness, insufficient trained personnel, and inadequate policies and financing. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) obligates Member States to take effective measures to ensure personal mobility and access to assistive technologies, including prosthetics and orthotics. Since 2006, over 170 countries have ratified the CRPD, committing to providing affordable, high-quality assistive products. Despite this, only 5–15% of individuals who could benefit from assistive products have access to them. To address these challenges, WHO has launched the Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology (GATE) initiative, which aims to improve access to affordable, high-quality assistive products. WHO’s global disability action plan (2014–2021) and subsequent publications call on Member States to develop financing and procurement policies to ensure universal access to assistive products, including prosthetics and orthotics. The document highlights the importance of integrating prosthetics and orthotics services into health systems to strengthen universal health coverage and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It provides a roadmap for governments to develop national policies, plans, and programs for prosthetics and orthotics services of the highest standard. The standards cover four key areas of the health system: policy (governance, financing, and information), products (prosthetics and orthotics), personnel (workforce), and service provision. The introduction emphasizes the critical role of prosthetics and orthotics in respecting the human rights of individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations. It underscores the need for mobility and dexterity to enable full participation in society. The document also acknowledges the significant gap in access to assistive products and calls for urgent action to address this disparity. In summary, the WHO’s standards for prosthetics and orthotics aim to ensure that everyone in need, regardless of location, has access to these essential services. By implementing these standards, Member States can fulfill their obligations under the CRPD, improve health outcomes, and promote the well-being of individuals with disabilities.
